notes: New start: a new expedition now begins in Brightwater Harbor, the Lost Cause's home port. June asks whether you want test dive first: a guided run round the harbor that covers driving, the compass and gauges, boost and battery, lamps, ping, recording a survey, photographing an animal and finding it in the compendium, being hauled home, the workshop, and a practice mission towing her tool crate back on the tether. Then the ship sails north and lowers you into the Lantern Archipelago. You can skip the trials and sail straight there; your first photo and Sand Dollars carry over.

The test dive now takes you around the harbor on a course of glowing rings, with a column of light over the next one. The camera swings to show you where the next ring is, and June points you to the marker on your compass. She stops you at places that fit each lesson: rise and dive by the dock, depth at the little reef, boost across open water to the old barge, lamps inside its dark hull, ping out the far end, then the old ferry steps to record a survey and snap a fish, and her tool crate to tow home.
Test dive: the marker you're heading for pulses on the compass with a ripple around it, and June shows you the marker's icon in her speech bubble so you know what to look for.

Test dive: at the little reef June now gives a tour of your dashboard, one part at a time (depth gauge, battery, hull, where you are and your Sand Dollars, then your tools), with each part outlined on screen. Press Enter (A) for the next. Every line now stays up long enough to read, even when you've already done what she asks.
Test dive: the dashboard tour ends with June pointing you to Settings, where Interface has the other HUD styles and Wildlife sets how bold the animals are (Peaceful to Adventurous).
Test dive: the sub starts with its lamps off, and inside the dark barge June asks you to switch them on.

Test dive: June now walks you through the tether a step at a time with the keys for each: start aiming, pick the crate, pick where the rope leaves your sub and fire. Then she shows reel and let go for the tow. Holding Backspace while aiming the tether no longer skips the test dive.

Test dive: in the workshop June now gives a tour of each section (Garage, Upgrades, Paint, Equipment, Loadout and Fast travel), explaining each section as you open it yourself (LB / RB on a controller, or click the tabs), with the next section you haven't seen outlined. Her battery line now warns that when it runs out the sub slows to a crawl.
June's tutorial lines no longer say tools are bought: choosing and restocking tools has always been free.
New expeditions start with one empty tool slot instead of a free Flare. Pick tools for free in the workshop's Loadout, and June points out the empty slot during the test dive.
June's tool crate in the test dive is now the game's detailed equipment case, in her orange.
The photo lesson is easier: more of the harbor fish can be photographed, a school swims right by the ferry steps, and the camera frame is wider during the lesson.

The old ferry steps are now a real sunken stretch of harbor wall: dressed stone in courses, a flight of steps down to a landing with an iron handrail, timber fender piles, mooring rings, a bollard and a lamp post. The survey recorder now stands in plain view on the sand in front.

Brightwater Harbor is rebuilt: a sandy beach between rocky headlands with boulders along the tideline, a breakwater with a striped lighthouse, painted cottages along the dock and up the hill, a harbor office with a clock tower, rowboats, a jetty and nets, pines and leafy trees across the hills, and underwater seagrass, seaweed, kelp, sponges, small corals, starfish, shells and reef fish.
Brightwater Harbor is always clear and sunny at midday during the opening and the test dive. The clock and the weather start moving once the Lost Cause sails for the islands.
June's lines in the opening and the test dive are rewritten: clearer, friendlier and more fun.

The opening now makes the goal clear: explore every area, fill the compendium, record every survey and finish every mission; June no longer brings up the falling stars in the opening. When you first reach the Lantern Islands, whether you did the test dive or skipped it, June pops up to wish you luck and remind you of the job.

Brightwater Harbor is now an Italian Riviera fishing village: tall, narrow houses in sun-washed ochre, rose, peach and lemon with green shutters, climbing the hill on stone-walled terraces, a pink church with a bell tower, cafés with striped awnings and umbrellas on the quay, strings of lights, washing lines, painted fishing boats tied up along the wall, and stone pines, cypresses and olive trees on the hills.

Finishing the Lantern Archipelago (every animal, survey and mission) now plays a short scene aboard the Lost Cause: June congratulates you, then the ship sails you north to the Frostglass Shelf. On arrival she reminds you of the job there, and that you can pull up beside the ship and hold Interact any time to sail back to the Lantern Archipelago.

Adventurous: there is no station recovery on the Adventurous wildlife level. Holding Recover no longer hauls you back; it shows a short note instead, so you have to watch your battery and make your own way home. Peaceful and Gentle are unchanged. The controls list, the settings page and June's first-dive line say so.

Folding solar kit: the kit now does something. With it fitted, the battery charges slowly while you sit at the surface in daylight (about 0.1% a second at noon, so roughly 17 minutes from flat to full; less late in the day, nothing at night, under water or under ice). Subs without the kit no longer charge at the surface at all, so the battery only comes back at a station, from a spare cell or from the kit.

Upgrades now belong to the whole fleet: buy one once and it is fitted to every sub you own, and every sub you earn later arrives already upgraded. They cost a little more (40 / 80 / 120 Sand Dollars per stage, pressure hull 30 / 55 / 80), so upgrading everything costs about 1,300 instead of about 800 per sub. Existing saves keep their best level of each upgrade, now on every sub.

Two new premium upgrades: Racing thrusters (a fourth Thrusters stage, 250 Sand Dollars: much more top speed and push) and Deep-cycle cells (a third Battery stage, 120 Sand Dollars: about 40% more charge than Expedition cells). The torque prop switch stays available while Racing thrusters are still to buy.

Photo pay is simpler: each species pays its full amount once, for your first photo, plus a little extra if that first animal is a rarer color (up to +50%) or a big one (Large +15%, Record +40%). After that, each new color or size you add to your album is a small 5 Sand Dollar tip, not the whole payout again.
Speed: boost is now a real burst (about 1.6x cruise at every thruster stage; stock boost 12 m/s instead of 9.75).
New: hold Z to creep at a slow, quiet pace and sneak up on wildlife (rebindable; on a controller, squeeze the trigger gently). June teaches it in the test dive's photo lesson.
Speed gauges now read full only at your sub's real top boost speed, and rising or diving no longer pushes the needle past it. The Brass dial was pegged at 8 knots before.

Towing is rebuilt as real underwater physics. Cargo has weight and water drag, so it sinks, trails behind and below you, and drags along the sand (kicking up silt) unless you reel it up. The rope stretches a little and only ever pulls: slack line snaps taut with a thump and a jolt, you feel every tug through the sub, and heavier loads slow you down. The load swings and turns to trail behind its rope, glances off rocks, and pins you in place if it snags. Let go and it carries on with its own momentum before settling upright on the bottom.
Kelp only snags when a stalk actually reaches your propeller. Brushing kelp with the nose or sides of the hull just pushes it aside. The prompt now says "Kelp caught in the propeller".
Garage with keyboard and mouse works like a controller: the first click selects an item, a second click buys or fits it.

Interface settings: the HUD is now two choices. HUD style picks the look (Classic, Enamel Panel, Dive Computer, Cinematic, Field Notebook) and HUD detail picks how much it shows: Minimal (depth, power, hull and heading only), Standard (every reading, system and tool, without the keys) or Guided (Standard with the key written on each system and tool). Every style has all three. The old Compact style is folded into Classic Minimal.

Four new HUD styles: Enamel Panel, Dive Computer, Cinematic and Field Notebook. The Interface settings page is tidier: the per-part HUD switches are gone (every part shows), and the page just shows a big preview of the style you pick.

New Minimal HUD style: each part of the HUD appears only when it has something to tell you (diving, turning, a ping, low battery) and fades away again. Settings also has a HUD opacity slider. The radio settings moved to the Sound tab.

Enamel Panel HUD (was Brass Panel): restyled to match the game, built like the Minnow itself: a deep teal enamel board and plates in cream enamel trim, cream dial faces with dark teal markings and an orange needle, cream push-buttons that light orange when on. The dashboard is now a free-standing board a little above the bottom of the screen, only as tall as its dials (the leather strip and name plate are gone).

HUD: new visibility readout on every HUD style (Standard and Guided). It shows how far you can see clearly, which is also how far the camera can photograph. In dark water it follows your lamps, and it reads "dark" with the lamps off.
The faint "F1  all controls" reminder now shows in the top right at Standard and Guided HUD detail in every HUD style (it used to show only at Guided). Minimal still keeps the screen clear.

Settings: the HUD style setting shows a preview of every style at each detail level: a cruising sub over calm open water, with the scene softened so the HUD stands out, and a label naming what that detail level shows.
The sonar no longer prints AHEAD, and the Compact HUD's compass, sonar scope and corner readouts are much smaller and simpler.
A sonar ping no longer puts a ring and a beam of light on each thing it finds; the note at the top of the screen and the sonar scope still tell you what is there.
Wildlife alerts ("Moving away", "Investigating" and so on) no longer overlap the survey, chest, station or boarding prompts: those prompts now sit clear above the alert while it shows.

Developer mode has a new Enter fog option that lets your sub dive to 450 m, and two buttons on the Interface page: play the Lantern ending scene, and sail between the Lantern Archipelago and Frostglass Shelf.

Every animal is now an individual: each comes in a few color forms (with a striking rarest form, such as a golden kelp bass, a white humpback, a blue snow crab or a purple seahorse) and in Small, Typical, Large and Record sizes. Everyone in a party sees the same animal the same way, and the animals you are not looking at can come back as different individuals as the day goes on.

Camera: when it locks onto an animal, two small tags under the name show that individual's size (a four-step bar, Small to Record) and its color with how rare that color is (gray typical, green uncommon, blue rare, gold rarest), marked NEW if it isn't in your album yet. The label also shows exactly what the shot will pay.

Every fish in a school or bait ball can now be photographed, so a rare color or a record-size fish anywhere in the group counts (before, only some fish in each school did). The camera's lock ring now sits on the exact animal it picked instead of the middle of the frame, so in a school you can see which fish the size and color tags describe.

Camera: the viewfinder only asks you to center an animal you can actually see: close enough to make out, in its photo range at your zoom, lit, and not behind anything. It no longer names fish that are far off, a speck, or hidden.
The camera can't shoot through murky water however far you zoom, and below about 120 m an animal has to be in your lamps' reach unless it makes its own light.

Reef fish in the shoals around your sub can now be photographed (before, only a few scripted schools counted), and the shoals keep to their time of day: day fish shelter at night, lanternfish rise after dark.

The compendium keeps up to six photos of each animal. Click one on its card to make it the cover. The card also shows which colors and sizes you have photographed, and the rarest form and record size to look for. A rare color or a big animal pays a little extra on your first photo of that species, and later new colors and sizes are a small tip.

Compendium: the animal details card is tidier. A larger picture, the album row only once you have more than one photo, the name first, three plain rows for where, when and camera distance, and colors and sizes as chips with a count.
Compendium: one page for each rarity, so every animal of a kind is together, with four rarity tabs in place of the page arrow. Click a tab, press 1 to 4, or use LT / RT on a controller.

Sperm whale: a real sperm whale's skin. Deep, prune-like creases over the body behind the head, a paler, smoother head covered in scars (pale rake marks in twos and threes and little round sucker scars from squid), a white mouth and darker, browner coloring.

Ocean sunfish: a proper swimming stroke. The tall top and bottom fins sweep side to side together like a pair of wings, flexing toward the tips with the back edge trailing, instead of just folding in. The clavus trims as it goes, the little side fins flutter and the body sways gently against each stroke.

Twelve new animals in open water and the deep of the Lantern Archipelago: sardine bait balls, comb jellies and yellowfin tuna (Common); mahi-mahi under drifting kelp rafts, great barracuda and chambered nautilus (Uncommon); whale shark, scalloped hammerhead schools, blue shark, leatherback turtle and bluntnose sixgill shark (Rare); and one sperm whale (Legendary). Each keeps to a general area and depth, with only a few sites, none close to the start: the compendium says where to look.

Wildlife rebalanced from a full census: moray eels now live in dens in the reef rocks, harbor seals loaf in the island coves, the giant squid no longer waits over the cargo wreck, more oarfish and ocean sunfish roam open water, and several rarities moved to match how often each animal can really be found. The compendium's where and when now match.

Seagulls now live in flocks all over the archipelago, wheeling over the water and resting on it, instead of popping up around your sub as you cruise. They're in the compendium as a Common you can photograph from the surface.
New Common in the compendium: the glow jelly, the pink, blue and violet jellies drifting over the deep plains.

New Rare in the compendium: the seahorse. Fourteen of them potter about the new seagrass beds, dense fields of long green seagrass on the shallow shelves round the islands and near the start; slow down and look low among the grass.

Seahorses now swim properly, rowing with a fluttering dorsal fin and steering with their little side fins, and each keeps to its own sandy clearing in the seagrass so it never swims through the leaves.

The seahorse is rebuilt from a photograph of a real one: horse-like head and thick snout, arched neck, deep belly, and a tail that curls into a tight spiral. It hovers upright with the tail curled, and when it swims it leans forward and the tail uncurls and streams out behind.
Rebuilt garibaldi, lanternfish (now a slim silver fish with a huge eye and rows of glowing lights) and ocean sunfish; the moon jelly's gonads are lilac; great whites are bigger.

The comb jelly is rebuilt as a real comb jelly: a glass-clear body with two cupped lobes round the mouth, the pale gut and canals showing inside, and eight rows of comb plates with rainbow light running along them. The lobes slowly open and close.
The mahi-mahi is rebuilt: a blunt bull forehead, a long rayed fin from above the eye to the tail, a deep V tail, blue-green back, gold sides and small electric-blue spots.

Leatherback turtle: a new model. It was a stretched, recolored green turtle, scutes and all, and its swimming stroke bent the back of its shell. It is now built as a leatherback: a long teardrop back with seven raised keels and no scutes, dark leathery skin flecked with white, a big blunt head with the pink spot on its crown, very long front flippers and broad rear paddles. The back stays rigid while the flippers stroke.

Barracuda: the schools no longer hang in one spot. Each school now patrols a beat along its drop-off together, all facing the same way, cruising at about 2.4 m/s with slower spells and quick bursts. A school parts around your sub and closes up behind it; creep in and they let you to about 7 m, charge in and they scatter to about 13 m. They also steer round rocks.

Open-ocean animals roam: tuna, whale sharks, blue sharks, leatherbacks, sixgill sharks and the sperm whale used to swim one fixed loop over and over. They now wander their territory, turning both ways, and never swim the same line twice. Sardine balls, mahi-mahi, hammerheads, nautiluses, comb jellies and the barracuda patrols also vary their line and pace. A party still sees every animal in the same place.
The warm heart, the cold seep and the Midnight gardens vents use the knobbly mineral chimney too, without the glowing rings on top.

The old placeholder dome and brass mast in the vent field is gone, and the separate "The Well" survey is retired: the drowned freighter's survey covers the bottom of the Well. The Lantern Archipelago now has 19 surveys; anything already recorded still counts toward the new total.

The drowned freighter at the bottom of the Well is rebuilt as a real ship, the Sea Thrush: a proper hull with plating dented between the frames, weld seams and rust running down, torn steel and open holds at the break, corrugated containers, deck cranes, a forecastle with windlass and anchors, and a detailed bridge house with portholes, stairs, funnel, lifeboat davits, propeller and rudder.

The survey recorder is rebuilt as a proper field instrument: a horizontal pressure housing with bolted teal end flanges and a glass camera dome behind a brass bezel, clamped in a tubular cradle with a brass lifting handle, a side data panel with a screen and a swinging pointer, cable glands at the back, a hydrophone, and a caged beacon lantern. It stands on a sturdier tripod with clamp collars and rubber feet that still settle onto the seabed.

Black smokers: the vent field by the deep well and the giant Vent Crown use the knobbly mineral chimney, in vent rock with ochre, rust and pale streaks, crusted shelves and side spires, and a sooty crater at the top. Their plumes pour out fast: a churning jet at the mouth, a lighter smoke column that shows in the dark, and big bubbles streaming up quickly with a gush every few seconds.

Water: fixed the dark band on the sea surface (also on the title screen); the surface reflection now updates every frame. Reflections also behave like real water: ripples smear them into soft vertical streaks, they're slightly darker and bluer than the land, and they fade near the sub so you see down into the sea.

Sight and light: you now see about half as far, closer to a real sea. In clear water things are half faded at about 105 m and gone by about 205 m (it was 185 m and 380 m), and haze, storms and plankton blooms shorten that further. The sea is dimmer under haze and storm, night is properly dark so your lamps do the work (night photos need the lamps unless the animal glows), and the light now fades smoothly through sunset instead of jumping.

Deep water: a plankton bloom now stays in the top of the sea (it thins from 18 m and is gone by 60 m), so the deep is clear blue water instead of green murk. Open water is brighter overhead and deeper blue below, and the water starts turning blue from about 12 m down.

Color of the deep: deep rock and sand were painted violet. They now have their true colors (dark gray stone, pale beige silt), and the blue comes from the light instead: daylight turns bluer as you go down (from about 10 m, fully by 70 m) and the water is fully deep blue by 110 m. So the deep reads as a soft blue-gray by daylight, and your lamps show the real colors up close.
Weather: plankton blooms are much rarer (about 1 dive in 10 instead of most of them) and don't follow one murky spell with another; clear water is the most common again.

Currents now change over the day: each one strengthens, weakens and reverses with the tide (about every 12 hours) and slowly wanders sideways, so they are not always in the same place. The chart shows them as they are now.
The trench fog now fades into the ocean haze with distance like everything else, instead of showing clearly from far above.

Foliage pass: sea fans, branching and staghorn corals, tube and barrel sponges, coral shelves, eelgrass meadows, seaweed beds, drifting kelp rafts, dune grass, palms, pines and leafy island trees are all rebuilt the way they really grow, in the style of the giant kelp.

Deep-sea life rebuilt: sea pens with feathery leaves outlined in glowing beads, stalked feather stars with ten curling comb-like arms, striped lantern anemones with two rings of tentacles, tube worms with collared white tubes and feathery red plumes, and hydrothermal vents with mineral-banded chimneys, flanges, side spires and glowing seams.
The leviathan arch (the great whale skeleton) now lies along the slope it rests on, with its rib tips, tail, skull and flipper set into the sand, instead of hanging over the hillside.

The Marigold is rebuilt as one detailed wreck: a little wooden trawler with planked hull, a stove-in bow, barnacles, a wheelhouse with a smashed window and an open door, mast and rigging, trawl gallows with otter boards, a winch, a heap of net and her name on bow and stern. The second boat that stood inside her is gone, and the survey recorder now stands on clear sand off her stern.

The Lost Cause is far more detailed: hull plating and draft marks, a cream sheer stripe with a coral pinstripe and a proper rubbing strake, bolted portholes with eyebrows, rounded deckhouse windows, a slipway with gates and swim ladders, a planked deck with coiled lines, drums and gas bottles, and a deckhouse with a bridge visor, wipers, a horn, life rafts and a workboat.
The chart is lettered like a sea chart: region names in spaced capitals under the markers, basins and features in italics, named islands, and depth soundings when you zoom in.

Chart: the legend is easier to read and its hover boxes no longer overlap, your sub shows as a little top-down sub with a beam showing which way you face, and currents are drawn as flowing ribbons with arrowheads instead of dashed lines. Player name tags only appear in co-op.
Old Bathy: the bolts round its three small top windows no longer float off the window rings.

Shop photos for lights, arms, guards, antennas and trinkets: each fitting now faces the camera (most were shot from behind), is framed tightly on its own shape and fills its card. Arm photos leave out the bow rail and its hull struts so the arm itself is big.
Survey spotlight and rotating beacon: no more stands; each sits on a bolted base straight on the roof.

Roof fittings (pizza sign, taxi light, disco ball, spotlight, beacon) no longer float on the Old Bathy: a tower or hatch behind them used to lift them up; now they step forward clear of it and sit on the roof itself.
Disco ball: no more stand. It sits on a low motor puck straight on the roof (rubber foot, vents, a little green power light) and spins just above it.
Twinfin headlamps: like the Gulper's, one big lamp centered on each pontoon's nose, facing straight ahead, in a thick dark rim with a pale inner ring. The old angled lamps and their sockets are gone.

Minnow front window: clean edge (its rubber seal was being cut into a sawtooth) and a shallow, smooth nook about 25 cm deep, with a rounded corner into the back panel, a wooden shelf with a brass lip, and a small brass lamp hood. The trinket sits a little further forward.

Arm hardware where it meets the sub: the bow rail is now a machined steel rail (front channel, end caps, screws, zinc anode), braced to the hull by pinned struts with hex adjusters, bolted shoes that sit flat on the hull, and clamps round the rail. Jointed arms get a saddle with a geared slewing ring, a pinned shoulder yoke, a bolted elbow knuckle and a rotary wrist coupling; the scoop pivots in bolted rail clamps and the net on a small turntable.

Sample jars arm rebuilt in detail: a green wire crate with rubber-lined collars, a brass SPECIMENS plate and hinged swing arms, holding four clear jars you can see into: a lab jar with a coral sprig, a clamp jar with a seashell (its glass lid still pops open), a stoppered jar with a silver fish, and a brass-lidded jar with an urchin and a starfish. Each has a paper label.
Sediment scoop: the canvas bucket beside the scoop is gone.
Longfin and Fishbowl headlamps: each lamp now stands out from the hull on a short barrel with a chrome band, so the whole lamp shows. The hull used to cover their lower edges.
Old Bathy: its new front lamps now actually appear in their yokes under the float and light the way (they were being built at the center of the hull).

Fitting fixes across the fleet: the bow mount sits clear of the hull across its full width; the ice plow braces to its own clamp when the hull is out of reach; the lowered plow and figurehead sit a little lower under a scoop; tyres and rope fenders hang a little further out; pool noodles keep a little more gap; the fish figurehead stands further off the bow; the Terrapin's wrap-around bumper posts meet the hull at both rails; the Gulper's deck sits a touch higher.
Two new lights in the shop: a Pizza delivery sign (a red roof sign with lit PIZZA panels and a pepperoni slice front and back) and a Taxi light (a glowing yellow TAXI roof light with a checker band).

Bumper bars: the chrome rail no longer pokes out of the black rubber sleeve; it stops where the rubber begins and tucks inside it. On the Terrapin's wrap-around bumper the chrome strip is set into the top of the sleeve and stops short of the rounded ends.

Festoon lights now keep out of the way of other fittings: on subs where they wrap the pods (Gulper, Hermit and the like) the cable tucks under the side guards, fins and deck load instead of running through them, the post-mounted strings sit outside the widest deck loads, and the aft post steps clear of the stabilizer fins.

Trail lanterns now burn for about six minutes of diving (the clock pauses at the surface, docked and in menus). Over the last minute and a half they dim and turn red, sputter at the very end, then fold their legs, tip over and sink into the silt, and their chart marker goes with them. Up to six still burn at once.
Minnow: the big front porthole is now clear glass looking into a small lit nook, and your trinket sits on a shelf inside it (like the Longfin's nose window), instead of on the roof.

Fitting fixes: with a bow arm fitted, the ice breaker plow and the fish figurehead now sit lower so the arm works above them (like the bumper bars opening). On the Fishbowl the bow mount and arms sit out in front of the glass bowl instead of inside it. On the Terrapin the festoon lights stop short of the antenna instead of running through it.

Bow arms now come alive. When you hook something with the tether, recover salvage or a star chest, or record a survey, your arm does its job: the claw reaches down and snaps shut, the grabber closes its fingers, the leaf blower blasts a puff of silt, the paint brush paints, the scoop digs, a sample jar pops its lid and the net sweeps the water. After a photo, or when a recovery is delivered, the arm gives a wave.
The Photo of June trinket now holds June's real portrait, printed in its cream mount, instead of a painted sketch.

The new equipment is rebuilt with much more detail: a disco ball with real mirror tiles, pleated paper lanterns, a jointed rubber glove, a finned leaf blower, a dripping paint brush and can, a molded ice plow, ridged foam noodles with buckles, a sewn wind sock, a concave satellite dish, hollow anemometer cups, a stave-built hot tub, a full vegetable bed, a crate of real bottles and detailed trinkets.
Trail lanterns are much brighter: each one now lights a wide patch of seabed (about twice the reach), with a warm glow and haze around the bulb that you can spot down the trail.

18 new equipment items in the shop. Lights: a spinning disco ball that throws pink, teal and gold spots, and swaying paper lanterns. Arms: a grabber hand, a leaf blower with a spinning fan, and a giant paint brush. Guards: an ice breaker plow (bow protection) and pool noodles (side protection). Masts: a wind sock, a satellite dish that looks about, a spinning anemometer and a Jolly Roger. Deck: a lit hot tub, a garden planter and a crate of message bottles. Trinkets: a lava lamp, a hula dancer, fuzzy dice and a plush octopus.

The Fishbowl gets proper round headlamps on its side pods (housing, chrome bezel, silvered reflector, domed lens and brow) in place of the flat white discs, and the Old Bathy gets a visible pair hanging under the float's nose on yokes; its light now comes from them.

Tools rebuilt as proper equipment with real moving parts. The hull patch, battery cartridge and kelp cutter ride a small ROV-style service arm that unfolds from the hull flank, reaches its work point (its elbow ram sliding in and out) and folds away: the patch is pressed onto the hull, clamps and turns its lamp green, then stays there a while; the battery plugs into the hull, lights its charge segments one by one and drops the spent cell; the cutter reaches back to the propeller, spins up and throws shredded kelp. The salvage scanner is a deck mast that swings up, telescopes, opens three hydrophones and spins, sending out ping rings. The trail lantern sinks with a gentle swing, lands in a puff of silt, opens its legs and warms up. Lift bags are real parachute bags with webbing straps that fill smoothly from a crumpled bundle, with gas bubbling into the mouth, and slump or burst at the end. The flare and sonar are unchanged.

Pearlescent paints: Pearl white and Black pearl in the shop, Abalone for 20 species, Moonstone for 15 surveys and Mother of pearl for 30 chests. Each turns a second color as the hull curves away from you, with a soft rainbow sheen and fine sparkle under the clear coat; their paint chips show the shift too. Sunset fade now unlocks at 19 surveys, every Lantern survey.

Shop on a controller: LB / RB switch the top tabs, LT / RT switch the sub-tabs (Paint, Wraps and Decals, and the equipment types), and pushing the stick past the last item in a row turns to the next page (back past the first for the previous one), in the shop grids and the fleet register alike. F1, or VIEW on a controller, shows the shop controls. The hints along the bottom are now tidy keycaps, and in Paint, Equipment and the Garage a right-stick click zooms the preview (the triggers are busy there).

Shop: each Thrusters stage shows its cruise and boost speed in knots, the next-upgrade line shows the change (for example Cruise 20 → 24 kn, Boost 35 → 40 kn), and the Torque propeller says it adds pull, not speed.
Shop pictures: paints and wraps are shown as paint cards (wraps show the real pattern over your paint), decals as their own inked artwork, and tools as ink drawings.
Wraps now fit the ballast tubes of the Hermit and Skipjack, and on the Needle and the Bell they cover the whole hull (they used to show only on the narrow lower band).

Headlamps: the Hermit, Skipjack, Needle, Bell, Longfin and Terrapin have new round headlamps (dark housing, chrome bezel, silvered reflector, glowing lens and a little brow) in place of the small flat ones.
Hermit and Barnacle: the work beacon is now a proper caged lamp on a bolted brass flange, and the grab rail is a polished brass tube with rounded bends on bolted feet.
Deck kit on the Barnacle, Hermit and Needle now sits low on a molded cradle instead of a tall stand: on the Barnacle's rear shelf, in the Hermit's aft well, and tilted to follow the Needle's tail.
The Hermit's station bunting now runs to the end of the back railing and is tied to the post.
Festoon string lights on the Gulper, Twinfin and Hermit now spiral round the ballast tanks instead of standing on posts on top.
The Longfin's nose window is now clear glass with a little lit nook behind it, and your trinket sits on a shelf inside where you can see it.
Fixed the station bunting flashing all its flags for a moment when you changed other equipment; it now only ever shows the flags you've earned.
Controllers now work in multiplayer: once you open Dive with friends or join a party, the game reads your pad through Steam Input with its own button layout instead of losing it.

Fixed party subs vanishing after a bump: a sub could end up stuck inside another one (most often after a lag spike). Hulls now always push each other back out the short way and can't be driven inside or through each other.

Shared waypoints: a waypoint you set on the chart now shows for everyone in your party, on their compass, as a ring in the water and on their chart, in your crewmate color. Crewmates' subs show on the chart too, and clicking a friend's waypoint on the chart makes it yours.
In a party, the workshop and station screens now show only your own sub, instead of everyone's subs docked inside each other in the same bay. Crewmates reappear when you head back out.

Co-op: the ocean's wildlife now stays in step for everyone in a party. Fish, schools and jellies follow the host's clock, the host plans the routes of the big roaming animals, and animals react to every sub in the party, not just yours.

Co-op: octopuses now take the same foraging trips on everyone's screen and hide from whichever sub startles them, the distant passing shoals stay at fixed spots for the whole party instead of following each player, and the lighthouse and dock gulls fly the same circles for everyone.

Less pop-in: the seabed, reef life and fish schools ahead of you now load further out (out to about 150-220 m), so they are already there, faint in the haze, as you arrive. Things beside and behind you load closer in and last, to save work.

Smoother play: the deep plains no longer stutter as a new patch of glowing life loads (it is built a little at a time), and under water the game no longer draws anything past the point where the haze hides it completely, about half as many draw calls on the reef.
The game now uses American spelling throughout (color, gray, meters, harbor).

The abyssal trench: past the sentinel stones a terraced canyon drops through a thick bank of fog at 350-395 m into a dark world of glowing lanterns, vent chimneys and a brine pool. A 350 m hull is crushed inside the fog.
A new legendary lives below the fog, with its own ambience and calls. Photograph it for the Trench Stalker achievement.
The Abyssal Seal: once every other animal is in the compendium, star chests hold a secret upgrade that gives one fully upgraded sub +100 m. Star chests are rarer.
Octopuses: a new species living in rocky dens near caves around the archipelago. They hunt, swim by jet, hide when you come close and ink when startled.
The octopus's garden is now a new landmark: a sunken seaplane, nosed into the sand with its cargo spilled.
Kelp rebuilt to look like real giant kelp, with long ruffled blades streaming in the current.
New camera viewfinder: focus brackets, exposure readouts, focal length, a shutter blink and the shot slides in as a print.
The compendium is grouped by rarity: Common, Uncommon, Rare, Legendary.
Smoother, more natural animation for the giant squid and other animals.
Fixes and polish: garage lighting, the Gulper and Hermit subs, the shop and achievements.
Smoother play: subs load faster with much lighter models, and fewer hitches while cruising, near stations and on the surface.
Rocks and reefs stream in further away, so less popping into view.
"Quiet" graphics is now genuinely lighter for laptops; new Settings > Display > Show performance stats.
Lighting: rock undersides catch light bounced off the sand, and jellies, bubbles and lamp beams no longer wash out against open water.
Wildlife: reworked glow jellies, rays that swim like rays, a heavier great white, and fish schools that move naturally and avoid rocks.
Red flare overhaul: ignition flash, flickering red glow, sparks and a rising smoke plume.
Tether: a real braided rope, a choice of where it leaves the sub, and a simpler picker.
Co-op: subs bump each other with real weight and momentum.
Sonar ping now charts the area around you (70 m at home, 120 m offshore).
Surface: rebuilt lighthouse, cottages, dock, rowboat, palms and pines.
Controls: safari camera moved to C; on a controller, LB + right stick zooms the camera and RT / LT zoom the safari camera; new boost card on the speed dial.
HUD and menus: a new controls card, clearer top-corner text, smoother dials, Settings buttons and a tidier mission log.
Fixed: dark squares and dots under water, the sub getting stuck in shallow water, shells on station decks, Terrapin hull flicker, floating arch legs, and camera jumps in rear view.
Tethering rebuilt: press tether to see snap points in reach, step through them, press again to attach. Cleaner glowing cable with a clamp.
Controller: RB is now the tether (tap to attach or release, hold to reel) and a click of the left stick toggles boost.
New sonar ping: a soft wave that runs along the seabed, glints on chests, surveys, stations, recoveries and animals, and a note of what it found.
Falling stars now leave rare glowing star chests. A star gives a direction and a search circle on the chart, and the chest hums when you are close.
Star chests pay 60 / 120 / 250 sand dollars and are rarer.
Missions: notebook-style notices and details page, details open with the interact key, and jobs beyond your pressure rating are locked.
Shop on a controller: moving over an item previews it, A fits it, X / Y change category, A fits upgrades.
Chart: left stick moves the view, softer view cone, smooth island edges, tidier header and buttons.
Chest, station and scenic stop prompts use the same dial card as recording a survey.
Unlocks are spread across the whole expedition instead of the first few surveys.

Fixed: offshore fish that were blank and frozen, sonar not firing while moving on a controller, kelp growing through station platforms, the Fishbowl's floor poking through its dome, overlapping prompts near stations.
Steering is inverted while reversing, like a car.
Postcard mode removed. US English spelling throughout.
Tethering rebuilt: press tether to see snap points in reach, step through them, press again to attach. Cleaner glowing cable with a clamp.

Fixed: offshore fish that were blank and frozen, sonar not firing while moving on a controller, kelp growing through station platforms, the Fishbowl's floor poking through its dome, overlapping prompts near stations.
Steering is inverted while reversing, like a car.
Postcard mode removed. US English spelling throughout.
The caves now look like natural rock outcrops that match the stone around them, instead of long tubes.
Four new dead-end caves to find in the Lantern Archipelago, each with one mouth and glowing fans at the back.
New sound above the water: gulls in fair weather, wind, rain and thunder in storms, and waves washing on the island shores.
The blue whale now has a call, and the water sounds are a little louder.
Five new calm piano tracks on the radio.
New guided first dive: June talks you through the controls one at a time, a first survey, a first animal photo and the trip home to the workshop. Hold Backspace to skip it.
June has a new portrait and an animated speech bubble, with a soft talking sound as her words appear.
The briefing is shorter: the control cards moved into the first dive.
Surveys, landmarks, unlocks, chests and new subs now arrive as small notebook slips on the left, each with its own icon. The large centre text is gone.
The song and artist now show under the map name while the radio is on.
Subs float at the right height on the surface.
The whale bones are rebuilt as a proper skeleton and renamed "The leviathan arch".
The up/down speed readout under the depth gauge is removed.
New opening: the R.V. Lost Cause, a briefing from June and the sub launch, in daylight. Enter or A moves on, Esc skips.
Finish everything in the Lantern Archipelago, then board the ship to sail to Frostglass Shelf. The old portal is gone.
Clean title cards for discoveries, landmarks and unlocks.
Distant land on the horizon is now clean layered silhouettes.
Stations are named: Lantern station is home, the others are "<name> station".
Sub models detailed: Longfin, Needle, Bell, Twinfin. Terrapin rebuilt as a domed sub. Hermit slimmed down. Fishbowl hatch fixed.
New cabin interiors on eight subs: proper pilot seats, control yokes, displays, gauges and pedals.
Bow arms, the bumper and the halo lights no longer run through each other; the bumper opens into two rails when an arm is fitted.
